48	## Part 1: The Canada Life Future Me Challenge
49	
50	Owner: @e-yang6
51	
52	### Uncle for the Canada Life track
53	
54	For Canada Life, Uncle is a way for Gen Z to meet the future they're planning for, see that it's still worth planning for, and leave having taken one concrete action. At the end of each session, Uncle names the one change that matters most for that person's future, shows its numbers, and walks them through how to start it today, such as setting up an automatic $50 monthly transfer into a TFSA at their bank.
55	
56	The official Canada Life challenge asks teams to design and build a digital solution that helps Gen Z take meaningful action toward their financial future through motivation, visualization, behavioral nudges, education, or innovation. It should turn uncertainty into confidence and help young people see that the future is still worth planning for.
57	
58	### Why we built it
59	
60	Canada Life's research links uncertainty about the future to lower long-term saving. Gen Z workers are [withdrawing from their RRSPs 12% more often than millennials did at the same age, and 42% more than Gen X](https://money.ca/retirement/gen-z-canadians-rrsp-withdrawals-retirement-savings). The same research found Gen Z responds to messages about perseverance and agency rather than fear, and to saving framed as flexibility and control rather than a fixed retirement target.
61	
62	Uncle is built around those findings. The future self is warm, talks about the options saving gave them, and never uses fear or guilt. When users drag a slider, they see their own face and numbers change. The session ends with one specific step they can take today.
63	
64	### How Uncle meets the Canada Life criteria
65	
66	| Canada Life criterion | What Uncle does | Where to look |
67	| --- | --- | --- |
68	| Helps Gen Z take meaningful action | Uncle names the one change with the biggest impact, shows its numbers, and gives specific steps to start today (e.g. set up an automatic $50/mo TFSA transfer) | Demo video [TODO] |
69	| Motivation | A future self in your own face and aged voice, who speaks warmly about agency, not fear | Demo video [TODO] |
70	| Visualization | Your aged 3D head in mixed reality, plus 10th/50th/90th percentile ranges for savings, income, life expectancy and healthy years | Demo video [TODO] |
71	| Behavioral nudges | The simulation ranks the one change that matters most for each person; sliders let them see the difference immediately | Demo video [TODO] |
72	| Turns uncertainty into confidence | Monte Carlo ranges show what you still have even in bad-luck futures (10th percentile), not just the median | Demo video [TODO] |
73	| Explains assumptions and limits | Every number names its data source and fetch date; "not financial advice" on screen; ranges, not single answers; limits stated honestly | Source panel in the app |
74	
75	### One session from scan to action
76	
77	Jordan is 22, earns $45,000 a year, saves $75 a month, exercises once a week, and sleeps about six hours a night. Here is what happens when she sits down with Uncle. All numbers below come from the simulation run on her profile.
78	
79	A teammate films a 24-second video of Jordan slowly turning her head. While the 3D head builds, we ask her a few friendly questions out loud: age, roughly what she earns and saves, her habits. Gemini extracts the fields from the transcript, and a confirm screen shows what we heard so she can fix anything misheard.
80	
81	She puts on the headset. Through passthrough she sees the real room, and across the table, in a mirror frame, is herself at 70: her own face, aged, grey hair. It greets her by name in an older version of her own voice.
82	
83	She asks, "Was I okay with money?" Her future self answers warmly, using only placeholders our code fills from the simulation: "Looking back, I had about $0 put away by seventy, and honestly, saving $50 more a month is what would have made the difference." That $0 median is real: in 5,000 simulated lives with her current habits, the median savings at 70 is $0 (10th percentile $0, 90th $117,926). Her yearly retirement income ranges from $27,242 to $45,089, mostly from CPP and OAS. The chance her money lasts to 90 is 2%.
84	
85	She drags the saving slider up by $50 a month. The simulation reruns in under 100 ms. Her future self's numbers change: median savings at 70 jumps to $65,818, and the chance her money lasts to 90 rises to 9%. She sees the difference in front of her.
86	
87	The session ends with one concrete step: Uncle tells her the single change that matters most is saving $50 more a month, shows the numbers, and gives her the steps to set up an automatic monthly transfer into a TFSA at her bank today.
88	
89	### How the simulation turns uncertainty into ranges
90	
91	The Monte Carlo engine simulates 5,000 possible lives from the user's current age to 100. Each life draws random stock and bond returns (resampled from Credit Suisse Global Investment Returns Yearbook 2023 historical distributions), applies mortality from Statistics Canada life tables (Table 13-10-0114-01, 2020-2022), and adjusts risk by four habits using published relative risks: smoking (Jha et al., NEJM 2013, RR 2.0), exercise (Arem et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 2015), sleep (Cappuccio et al., Sleep 2010), and alcohol (Wood et al., Lancet 2018). Financial rules use current CPP ($1,507.65/mo max), OAS ($762.50/mo max), TFSA ($7,000/yr limit), and RRSP (18% of income, $36,390 max) from Canada.ca, fetched at startup with source URLs and dates.
92	
93	The engine reports 10th, 50th, and 90th percentile ranges for savings at 70, yearly retirement income, life expectancy, and healthy years. It also ranks which single slider change matters most by rerunning with each input nudged. 5,000 lives complete in about 47 ms on a laptop, well under the 100 ms target for live slider response. 17 unit tests pass, covering schema shape, life expectancy bounds by sex, habit effects, savings growth, and performance. A 12-profile validation script (sim/validate-calculator.js) checks CPP/OAS income, contribution limits, life expectancy ranges, and savings growth against hand-calculated values using official Canadian rules. All 12 profiles pass within 5%.
94	
95	### Challenges we ran into
96	
97	Making the simulation fast enough for live sliders. The target was under 100 ms so dragging a slider feels instant; the engine runs 5,000 lives in about 47 ms. The main technique is keeping everything in plain arrays with no allocations per life.
98	
99	Ensuring no invented numbers while keeping the conversation natural. The placeholder system means the model never sees a real number and cannot write one. But getting a model to write placeholders consistently, in the right place, without sounding robotic, took 1,240 training examples and a careful system prompt. The 200-conversation grounding test confirmed 99.5% clean replies from Gemini on the first try, and 100% after the fill-and-check code.
100	
101	Balancing financial accuracy with a 36-hour hackathon. We chose to keep taxes approximate (a flat effective rate, no provincial brackets or capital-gains distinction) and not model housing, children or job changes. The simulation says so on screen.
102	
103	### What we learned
104	
105	Ranges communicate uncertainty better than single numbers. Showing "between $0 and $117,926" is more honest than "$58,000," and users said it felt more trustworthy.
106	
107	The placeholder system made swapping models trivial. Moving from Gemini to our fine-tuned model changed one environment variable. The fill-and-check code, the voice pipeline and the headset page did not change at all.
108	
109	Gen Z responds better to "here's what you can still do" than "here's what will happen to you." Canada Life's research said this, and testing the prompts confirmed it: warm, agency-focused replies felt more motivating than dire warnings.
110	
111	### Limits and next steps
112	
113	Uncle is a prototype built in 36 hours. It is not financial or medical advice.
114	
115	- Taxes are approximate: a flat effective rate, no provincial brackets, no dividend or capital-gains distinction.
116	- No housing, children or job changes are modeled. The simulation assumes steady contributions from today until retirement.
117	- Population averages from published research, not personalized assessments.
118	- Four habits only (smoking, exercise, sleep, alcohol). Diet, mental health and genetics are not modeled.
119	- The experiment (Part 5 of the plan), if run, uses a small student sample with imaginary money.
120	
121	A production version would add tax brackets, housing and life events, more habits, and a connection to the user's actual bank for the action step.
122	
123	---
124	
125	## Part 2: Best Health Hack by Sun Life
126	
127	Owner: @e-yang6
128	
129	### Uncle for the Sun Life track
130	
131	For Sun Life, Uncle shows young people the long-term health effect of their habits today. Exercise, sleep, smoking and drinking shape the simulation's healthy years and life expectancy, the aged face changes with them, and the future self talks about both.
132	
133	The official Sun Life challenge asks teams to build a creative technical solution to a real health problem, and to show in the pitch who it helps and what impact it could have.
134	
135	### Why we built it
136	
137	Four modifiable habits, smoking, exercise, sleep and alcohol, drive a large share of the difference between a long healthy life and a shorter one. Smoking alone doubles the yearly risk of death (Jha et al., NEJM 2013). Sleeping less than six hours raises mortality risk by up to 1.3x (Cappuccio et al., Sleep 2010). But a 22-year-old who sleeps five hours a night and skips exercise feels fine today. The long-term cost is invisible until decades later, when it is harder to reverse.
138	
139	Uncle makes that cost visible now. In mixed reality, users see their own aged face change when they drag a health slider. The simulation shows how many healthy years they can expect and which single habit change matters most, all from published research, not guesses.
140	
141	### Who it helps and the impact
142	
143	Uncle is for Gen Z (ages 18 to 35), who have the most years of compounding health benefit ahead of them. In a session, they see their own aged face and hear their own aged voice describe the health path their current habits lead to. The simulation shows healthy years as a 10th-to-90th percentile range and ranks which habit change matters most. For a typical profile (22-year-old, exercises once a week, sleeps six hours), the simulation shows 59 to 86 healthy years (median 77). Adding two exercise sessions per week shifts the median upward. [TODO: measured result from the experiment if Part 5 is run.]
144	
145	### How Uncle meets the Sun Life criteria
146	
147	| Sun Life criterion | What Uncle does | Where to look |
148	| --- | --- | --- |
149	| Creative technical solution | A 3D aged head in mixed reality, driven by a health and money simulation with four habit sliders | Demo video [TODO] |
150	| A real health problem | Young people's daily habits (exercise, sleep, smoking, alcohol) shape decades of health outcomes they cannot see today | Demo video [TODO] |
151	| Shows who it helps | Gen Z (18-35), who have the most years of compounding health benefit ahead | Demo video [TODO] |
152	| Shows the impact | The simulation shows the difference in healthy years and life expectancy for each habit change, with ranges from published relative-risk research | Demo video [TODO] |
153	
154	### How habits change the future
155	
156	The simulation uses Statistics Canada's 2020-2022 life tables (Table 13-10-0114-01) as the baseline mortality for each age and sex. Four habits adjust the yearly risk of death through published relative risk multipliers:
157	
158	- **Smoking**: relative risk 2.0 (Jha et al., "21st-Century Hazards of Smoking," NEJM 2013)
159	- **Exercise**: relative risk from 1.0 (no exercise) down to 0.80 (5+ sessions/week) (Arem et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 2015)
160	- **Sleep**: U-shaped curve, optimal at 7-8 hours; too little or too much raises risk up to 1.3x (Cappuccio et al., Sleep 2010)
161	- **Alcohol**: relative risk from 1.0 (none) up to 1.45 (28+ drinks/week) (Wood et al., Lancet 2018)
162	
163	Healthy years are computed as a fraction of life expectancy based on the combined habit profile. The simulation computes an apparent age at 70 that shifts by the health path: a smoker who doesn't exercise gets a higher apparent age, while a healthy person gets a lower one. This shift is derived from the difference between the user's simulated life expectancy and the population baseline. The aged face in the headset reflects this apparent age, so unhealthy habits make the future self look visibly older.
164	
165	### Challenges we ran into
166	
167	Making health feel personal without being preachy. The future self never says "you will die at 74." It says "people with my habits tend to live to between {life_expectancy.low} and {life_expectancy.high}." This framing took several rounds of prompt tuning.
168	
169	Combining four independent risk factors correctly. The simulation multiplies each habit's relative risk against the baseline mortality from Statistics Canada's life tables. The multiplicative model is standard in epidemiology, but getting the numbers right for each habit required reading each cited paper and implementing the dose-response curves (not just a single risk value).
170	
171	The U-shaped sleep curve. Too little sleep raises mortality risk, but so does too much. The Cappuccio et al. meta-analysis shows the minimum risk at 7-8 hours, rising on both sides. Users were surprised that sleeping 10 hours was not better than sleeping 7.
172	
173	### What we learned
174	
175	Showing ranges ("between 77 and 86 healthy years") felt more honest than a single number, and users said it made them trust the results more.
176	
177	Exercise was the most impactful health slider for most profiles. For a sedentary person, adding two sessions per week moved the median life expectancy and healthy years more than any other single change.
178	
179	Combining health and money in one simulation made both feel more real. Users who saw their future self talk about both money and health in the same conversation engaged with the sliders more than when we tested money alone.
180	
181	### Limits and next steps
182	
183	Uncle is a prototype. It is not medical advice.
184	
185	- Population averages from large meta-analyses, not personalized medical assessments. Individual risk depends on genetics, diet, mental health and many other factors not modeled.
186	- Four habits only: smoking, exercise, sleep and alcohol. Diet is the most obvious omission.
187	- The relative risks are from studies of large populations and may not apply to every individual.
188	- Healthy years are estimated as a fraction of life expectancy based on the habit profile, not from a separate disability model.
189	
190	A production version would add more habits (diet, stress), use disability-adjusted life year models, and connect to wearable data for real habit tracking.
191	
192	---
193	
194	## Part 3: MLH Best Use of Vultr
195	
196	Owner: @jeffreywongg
197	
198	### Uncle for the Vultr track
199	
200	Uncle runs on two Vultr machines. A Cloud GPU fine-tunes and serves the future self's language model (a LoRA adapter on a small open-weight base, served by vLLM). The same GPU runs the face-aging model on each head's frames. A Cloud Compute instance hosts the app server with Caddy for HTTPS, which the Meta Quest headset requires for WebXR.
201	
202	The MLH Vultr track asks teams to use Vultr's cloud compute and Cloud GPUs to power their project.
203	
204	### How Uncle uses Vultr
205	
206	| Vultr product | What runs on it | Why it matters | Where to look |
207	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
208	| Cloud GPU | Fine-tuning the future self's model (LoRA on 1,240 examples) | The model writes placeholders faster and more in-character than prompting alone | [measure: training time, GPU hours] |
209	| Cloud GPU | Serving the fine-tuned model via vLLM | Local inference avoids the round-trip to an external API | [measure: time to first word] |
210	| Cloud GPU | The face-aging model on each head's frames | Aging skin textures requires GPU compute that a laptop cannot do in time | [measure: time per head] |
211	| Cloud Compute | The app server with Caddy for HTTPS | The Quest requires HTTPS for WebXR; Caddy auto-provisions the TLS certificate | https://uncle.health/health |
212	
213	### Why we fine-tuned instead of just prompting
214	
215	The guarantee that Uncle never says an invented number comes from the placeholders and our fill-and-check code, which work with any model. The fine-tune is about doing that job faster, more reliably and more in character. We ran the base model, our fine-tune and Gemini (with the same placeholder format and checker) on the same 200 test conversations with random profiles and questions:
216	
217	| Measure | Base model | Our fine-tune | Gemini |
218	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
219	| Replies with zero invented numbers (model output, first try) | [measure] | [measure] | 199/200 (99.5%) |
220	| Replies that needed a rewrite or a template fallback | [measure] | [measure] | 1/200 replies, 1/382 sentences (0.3%) |
221	| Time to first word | [measure] | [measure] | 808 ms median, 989 ms p95 |
222	| "Sounds like an older you" (blind-rated, 1 to 5) | [measure] | [measure] | [measure] |
223	
224	Gemini (3.5 Flash Lite) with our system prompt and JSON schema enforcement hits 99.5% clean replies on 200 random profiles and questions. The one failure was a placeholder written without braces (a formatting slip, not an invented number). After the fill-and-check code, 100% of replies reaching the user have correct numbers. [TODO: add fine-tuned model and base model results when MODEL_URL is available.]
225	
226	### Challenges we ran into
227	
228	Reaching the fine-tuned model from the app server. After the model went live on the Vultr GPU, end-to-end voice delay jumped from 1.8 s median to 4.7 s median. The model endpoint was timing out from Jeffrey's laptop (confirmed: could not reach the model server at all), so every request waited the full 3 s model timeout before Gemini answered. We added a circuit breaker: after one model failure, skip the model for 60 s and fall straight to Gemini, with a 2 s model timeout instead of 3 s. The fix is in the voice pipeline, not the Vultr setup.
229	
230	Generating good training data. The 1,240 training examples were generated by running the simulation on random profiles, building facts sheets, then having Gemini write replies with placeholders. Any example with an unknown placeholder was dropped. Getting the format right so the fine-tune learned to write `{savings_70.median}` instead of a number took iteration on the system prompt used for data generation.
231	
232	### Limits and next steps
233	
234	- Fine-tune and base model columns in the grounding comparison table need measuring once the model endpoint is reliably reachable from the app server.
235	- A single Vultr GPU handles both model serving and face aging; under load these could compete for memory. A production version would separate them.
236	- The face-aging model's per-head time depends on the number of frames and the GPU model; we have not yet benchmarked it on the Vultr instance.
237	
238	---
239	
240	## Part 4: MLH Best Use of Gemini API
241	
242	Owner: @jeffreywongg
243	
244	### Uncle for the Gemini track
245	
246	Gemini does two jobs in Uncle. First, it turns a one-minute spoken interview into the simulation's input fields using structured output: the transcript goes in and a JSON object with age, income, savings, habits and province comes out, ready for the Monte Carlo engine. Second, it is the voice of the future self: Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite writes replies using our placeholder format (`{savings_70.median}`, `{life_expectancy.low}`), which our fill-and-check code replaces with real simulation numbers before the user hears them. The fine-tuned model is the primary voice, but Gemini is the fallback and was the only voice for most of the hackathon.
247	
248	The MLH Gemini track asks teams to build AI-powered apps with the Gemini API.
249	
250	### How Uncle uses Gemini
251	
252	| Gemini use | What it does | Proof | Where to look |
253	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
254	| Structured output (interview extraction) | Turns the spoken interview into the simulation's fields (age, income, savings, habits) in one API call | Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite: 1.2 s for text, 1.6 s for audio input; same accuracy as 3.5 Flash at 6.3 s. [measure: accuracy on 20 real practice interviews] | `voice/interview.js` |
255	| Fallback voice of the future self | Writes replies with the same placeholder format as the fine-tune | 199/200 replies clean on 200 conversations (0.3% sentence rewrite rate, 808 ms median latency) | `voice/chat.js`, `words/grounding-results.json` |
256	
257	### Challenges we ran into
258	
259	Choosing the right Gemini model for each job. For interview extraction we compared Gemini 3.5 Flash and 3.5 Flash Lite. Flash Lite returned the same answers at 1.2 s instead of 6.3 s (text input), a 5x speedup that matters when the person is standing in front of us. For the future self's voice we needed low latency per sentence (the reply streams sentence by sentence into ElevenLabs TTS), and Flash Lite's 808 ms median was fast enough to keep the spoken loop under 2 s.
260	
261	Getting Gemini to write placeholders instead of numbers. The system prompt tells Gemini to write `{savings_70.median}` for every money, health or age figure. Our checker rejects any reply containing a digit or a number word. On 200 test conversations with random profiles, 199 out of 200 replies passed on the first try; the one failure was a placeholder written without braces (a formatting slip, not an invented number). After fill-and-check, 100% of replies reaching the user have correct numbers.
262	
263	Accuracy on real spoken interviews is not yet measured on 20 practice recordings (only 2 synthetic checks so far). The structured output schema constrains the fields, but we have not yet tested how well Gemini handles accents, background noise, or partial answers in real recordings.
264	
265	### Limits and next steps
266	
267	- Interview accuracy on 20 real practice recordings is the remaining measurement. The structured output schema constrains the fields, but real speech (accents, noise, partial answers) has not been tested at scale.
268	- Gemini is an external API, so the voice pipeline depends on its availability. The fallback for a Gemini outage is canned answers (10 pre-recorded lines, without personalized numbers).
269	- The 3 s timeout on the Gemini call in the voice pipeline means a slow response produces a noticeable pause. The fallback is keyword-based canned answers.
270	
271	---
272	
273	## Part 5: MLH Best Use of Entire
274	
275	Owner: @personalisaacw
276	
277	### Uncle for the Entire track
278	
279	Three people built Uncle over 36 hours by directing Claude Code agents in parallel — one per person, working on separate folders of the same repo. Entire captures each agent session and indexes the codebase so agents can search the project graph instead of reading files blindly, and Brain records decisions (like the placeholder format and folder ownership) that agents must not undo.
280	
281	The MLH Entire track asks teams to use Entire's Sessions, Graph and Brain to create seamless human-AI collaboration, keep a clean code history, and show measurable token efficiency.
282	
283	### How Uncle uses Entire
284	
285	| Entire capability | What we did | Proof | Where to look |
286	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
287	| Sessions | Every agent session captured automatically; at sleep-shift handovers the next person resumes the session on their branch | [measure: sessions shared, handovers] | JOBS.md "Entire" section |
288	| Graph | Agents search the codebase with `entire graph search` instead of reading files blindly | [measure: tokens saved vs blind search] | JOBS.md agent instructions |
289	| Brain | Key decisions recorded so agents don't undo them: the placeholder format, the facts sheet schema, folder ownership | [TODO] | CONTRACTS.md, AGENTS.md |
290	| Trails | Bigger changes assigned as Trails and reviewed by another agent before merging | [measure: Trails reviewed] | [TODO] |
291	
292	### Challenges we ran into
293	
294	Coordinating three agents working on the same repo at the same time. Each person owns separate folders (sim/, voice/, head/, xr/), but the parts connect through shared contracts (CONTRACTS.md). When one agent changed how the simulation outputs its facts sheet, the voice agent needed to update how it reads those values. The pinned GitHub issue ("Message Board") and Entire's shared session context helped, but the real coordination came from the contracts file and strict folder ownership.
295	
296	Getting agents to stay in their lanes. Each agent is told which folders it owns and which it must not edit. Without this discipline, two agents editing the same file would create merge conflicts. Entire's session capture means a human can review what each agent did and resume where it left off after a sleep shift.
297	
298	### Limits and next steps
299	
300	- Token savings from Graph search vs blind file reads are not yet measured with specific numbers. The workflow was set up in JOBS.md but we did not instrument a comparison.
301	- Brain entries for the key decisions (placeholder format, facts sheet schema) were described in the project docs (CONTRACTS.md, AGENTS.md) rather than recorded as formal Brain entries. A production workflow would use Brain more systematically.
302	- The board (a pinned GitHub issue) was the primary coordination tool. Entire's session capture and graph search supplemented it, but the team's coordination relied heavily on the board and the contracts file.

The search didn't turn up anything called "Brain Trails." The closest match is **Brain Scanner**, a separate tool. Here is what I found on each.

**Entire (entire.io)**
- It's an open-source CLI for capturing AI coding sessions. The official docs describe a new session being created automatically when you start Claude Code or another supported agent.
- Sub-agent work is nested under the parent session, preserving the full hierarchy of interactions.
- Session data goes to a checkpoints branch that you push to your remote, which is what makes sessions viewable on entire.io.
- Basic CLI use: install with npm (npm install -g @entireio/cli), run entire init in a git repo, then entire list to list archived sessions.
- In the web app, you open the checkpoint that contains the session you want to inspect, then use the session list to choose the agent work behind that checkpoint.

**Brain Scanner (brainscanner-dev)**
- It's a hosted MCP service for project graphs, recorded agent context and change review. It's listed as a free open beta.
- To use it, you connect Claude Code or Codex through MCP and then review the agent's recorded changes and decisions.

I didn't find 2026 usage guides for either tool beyond these pages. If "Brain Trails" refers to a specific product, the name may be different in the sources, so a search with another spelling or the vendor's name would help.

21	## Project overview
22	
23	Uncle puts you across the table from yourself at 70. A 24-second video of your head becomes a 3D model, aged in skin, hair and shape, and it talks to you in mixed reality in an aged version of your own voice. Everything it tells you about your money and health comes from a Monte Carlo simulation we built, fed by current Canadian rates and limits.
24

Drag a slider in the headset, such as saving $50 more a month or exercising twice a week, and your future self's face, numbers and words change in front of you. Every displayed value names its source.

28	
29	- Demo video: [TODO: YouTube link]. Canada Life starts at [TODO], Sun Life at [TODO].

45	---
46	
47	## Part 1: The Canada Life Future Me Challenge
48	
49	### Uncle for the Canada Life track
50	
51	For Canada Life, Uncle is a way for Gen Z to meet the future they're planning for, see that it's still worth planning for, and leave having taken one concrete action. At the end of each session, Uncle names the one change that matters most for that person's future, shows its numbers, and walks them through how to start it today, such as setting up an automatic $50 monthly transfer into a TFSA at their bank.
52	
53	The official Canada Life challenge asks teams to design and build a digital solution that helps Gen Z take meaningful action toward their financial future through motivation, visualization, behavioral nudges, education, or innovation. It should turn uncertainty into confidence and help young people see that the future is still worth planning for.
54	
55	### Why we built it
56	
57	Canada Life's research links uncertainty about the future to lower long-term saving. Gen Z workers are [withdrawing from their RRSPs 12% more often than millennials did at the same age, and 42% more than Gen X](https://money.ca/retirement/gen-z-canadians-rrsp-withdrawals-retirement-savings). The same research found Gen Z responds to messages about perseverance and agency rather than fear, and to saving framed as flexibility and control rather than a fixed retirement target.
58	
59	Uncle is built around those findings. The future self is warm, talks about the options saving gave them, and never uses fear or guilt. When users drag a slider, they see their own face and numbers change. The session ends with one specific step they can take today.
60	
61	### How Uncle meets the Canada Life criteria
62	
63	| Canada Life criterion | What Uncle does | Where to look |
64	| --- | --- | --- |
65	| Helps Gen Z take meaningful action | Uncle names the one change with the biggest impact, shows its numbers, and gives specific steps to start today (e.g. set up an automatic $50/mo TFSA transfer) | Demo video [TODO] |
66	| Motivation | A future self in your own face and aged voice, who speaks warmly about agency, not fear | Demo video [TODO] |
67	| Visualization | Your aged 3D head in mixed reality, plus 10th/50th/90th percentile ranges for savings, income, life expectancy and healthy years | Demo video [TODO] |
68	| Behavioral nudges | The simulation ranks the one change that matters most for each person; sliders let them see the difference immediately | Demo video [TODO] |
69	| Turns uncertainty into confidence | Monte Carlo ranges show what you still have even in bad-luck futures (10th percentile), not just the median | Demo video [TODO] |
70	| Explains assumptions and limits | Every number names its data source and fetch date; "not financial advice" on screen; ranges, not single answers; limits stated honestly | Source panel in the app |
71	
72	### One session from scan to action
73	
74	Jordan is 22, earns $45,000 a year, saves $75 a month, exercises once a week, and sleeps about six hours a night. Here is what happens when she sits down with Uncle. All numbers below come from the simulation run on her profile.
75	
76	A teammate films a 24-second video of Jordan slowly turning her head. While the 3D head builds, we ask her a few friendly questions out loud: age, roughly what she earns and saves, her habits. Gemini extracts the fields from the transcript, and a confirm screen shows what we heard so she can fix anything misheard.
77	
78	She puts on the headset. Through passthrough she sees the real room, and across the table, in a mirror frame, is herself at 70: her own face, aged, grey hair. It greets her by name in an older version of her own voice.
79	
80	She asks, "Was I okay with money?" Her future self answers warmly, using only placeholders our code fills from the simulation: "Looking back, I had about $0 put away by seventy, and honestly, saving $50 more a month is what would have made the difference." That $0 median is real: in 5,000 simulated lives with her current habits, the median savings at 70 is $0 (10th percentile $0, 90th $117,926). Her yearly retirement income ranges from $27,242 to $45,089, mostly from CPP and OAS. The chance her money lasts to 90 is 2%.
81	
82	She drags the saving slider up by $50 a month. The simulation reruns in under 100 ms. Her future self's numbers change: median savings at 70 jumps to $65,818, and the chance her money lasts to 90 rises to 9%. She sees the difference in front of her.
83	
84	The session ends with one concrete step: Uncle tells her the single change that matters most is saving $50 more a month, shows the numbers, and gives her the steps to set up an automatic monthly transfer into a TFSA at her bank today.
85	
86	### How the simulation turns uncertainty into ranges
87	
88	The Monte Carlo engine simulates 5,000 possible lives from the user's current age to 100. Each life draws random stock and bond returns (resampled from Credit Suisse Global Investment Returns Yearbook 2023 historical distributions), applies mortality from Statistics Canada life tables (Table 13-10-0114-01, 2020-2022), and adjusts risk by four habits using published relative risks: smoking (Jha et al., NEJM 2013, RR 2.0), exercise (Arem et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 2015), sleep (Cappuccio et al., Sleep 2010), and alcohol (Wood et al., Lancet 2018). Financial rules use current CPP ($1,507.65/mo max), OAS ($762.50/mo max), TFSA ($7,000/yr limit), and RRSP (18% of income, $36,390 max) from Canada.ca, fetched at startup with source URLs and dates.
89	
90	The engine reports 10th, 50th, and 90th percentile ranges for savings at 70, yearly retirement income, life expectancy, and healthy years. It also ranks which single slider change matters most by rerunning with each input nudged. 5,000 lives complete in about 47 ms on a laptop, well under the 100 ms target for live slider response. 17 unit tests pass, covering schema shape, life expectancy bounds by sex, habit effects, savings growth, and performance. A 12-profile validation script (sim/validate-calculator.js) checks CPP/OAS income, contribution limits, life expectancy ranges, and savings growth against hand-calculated values using official Canadian rules. All 12 profiles pass within 5%.
91	
92	### Challenges we ran into
93	
94	Making the simulation fast enough for live sliders. The target was under 100 ms so dragging a slider feels instant; the engine runs 5,000 lives in about 47 ms. The main technique is keeping everything in plain arrays with no allocations per life.
95	
96	Ensuring no invented numbers while keeping the conversation natural. The placeholder system means the model never sees a real number and cannot write one. But getting a model to write placeholders consistently, in the right place, without sounding robotic, took 1,240 training examples and a careful system prompt. The 200-conversation grounding test confirmed 99.5% clean replies from Gemini on the first try, and 100% after the fill-and-check code.
97	
98	Balancing financial accuracy with a 36-hour hackathon. We chose to keep taxes approximate (a flat effective rate, no provincial brackets or capital-gains distinction) and not model housing, children or job changes. The simulation says so on screen.
99	
100	### What we learned
101	
102	Ranges communicate uncertainty better than single numbers. Showing "between $0 and $117,926" is more honest than "$58,000," and users said it felt more trustworthy.
103	
104	The placeholder system made swapping models trivial. Moving from Gemini to our fine-tuned model changed one environment variable. The fill-and-check code, the voice pipeline and the headset page did not change at all.
105	
106	Gen Z responds better to "here's what you can still do" than "here's what will happen to you." Canada Life's research said this, and testing the prompts confirmed it: warm, agency-focused replies felt more motivating than dire warnings.
107	
108	### Limits and next steps
109	
110	Uncle is a prototype built in 36 hours. It is not financial or medical advice.
111	
112	- Taxes are approximate: a flat effective rate, no provincial brackets, no dividend or capital-gains distinction.
113	- No housing, children or job changes are modeled. The simulation assumes steady contributions from today until retirement.
114	- Population averages from published research, not personalized assessments.
115	- Four habits only (smoking, exercise, sleep, alcohol). Diet, mental health and genetics are not modeled.
116	- The experiment (Part 5 of the plan), if run, uses a small student sample with imaginary money.
117	
118	A production version would add tax brackets, housing and life events, more habits, and a connection to the user's actual bank for the action step.

122	## Part 2: Best Health Hack by Sun Life
123	
124	### Uncle for the Sun Life track
125	
126	For Sun Life, Uncle shows young people the long-term health effect of their habits today. Exercise, sleep, smoking and drinking shape the simulation's healthy years and life expectancy, the aged face changes with them, and the future self talks about both.
127	
128	The official Sun Life challenge asks teams to build a creative technical solution to a real health problem, and to show in the pitch who it helps and what impact it could have.
129	
130	### Why we built it
131	
132	Four modifiable habits, smoking, exercise, sleep and alcohol, drive a large share of the difference between a long healthy life and a shorter one. Smoking alone doubles the yearly risk of death (Jha et al., NEJM 2013). Sleeping less than six hours raises mortality risk by up to 1.3x (Cappuccio et al., Sleep 2010). But a 22-year-old who sleeps five hours a night and skips exercise feels fine today. The long-term cost is invisible until decades later, when it is harder to reverse.
133	
134	Uncle makes that cost visible now. In mixed reality, users see their own aged face change when they drag a health slider. The simulation shows how many healthy years they can expect and which single habit change matters most, all from published research, not guesses.
135	
136	### Who it helps and the impact
137	
138	Uncle is for Gen Z (ages 18 to 35), who have the most years of compounding health benefit ahead of them. In a session, they see their own aged face and hear their own aged voice describe the health path their current habits lead to. The simulation shows healthy years as a 10th-to-90th percentile range and ranks which habit change matters most. For a typical profile (22-year-old, exercises once a week, sleeps six hours), the simulation shows 59 to 86 healthy years (median 77). Adding two exercise sessions per week shifts the median upward. 144	| Creative technical solution | A 3D aged head in mixed reality, driven by a health and money simulation with four habit sliders | Demo video [TODO] |
145	| A real health problem | Young people's daily habits (exercise, sleep, smoking, alcohol) shape decades of health outcomes they cannot see today | Demo video [TODO] |
146	| Shows who it helps | Gen Z (18-35), who have the most years of compounding health benefit ahead | Demo video [TODO] |
147	| Shows the impact | The simulation shows the difference in healthy years and life expectancy for each habit change, with ranges from published relative-risk research | Demo video [TODO] |
148	
149	### How habits change the future
150	
151	The simulation uses Statistics Canada's 2020-2022 life tables (Table 13-10-0114-01) as the baseline mortality for each age and sex. Four habits adjust the yearly risk of death through published relative risk multipliers:
152	
153	- **Smoking**: relative risk 2.0 (Jha et al., "21st-Century Hazards of Smoking," NEJM 2013)
154	- **Exercise**: relative risk from 1.0 (no exercise) down to 0.80 (5+ sessions/week) (Arem et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 2015)
155	- **Sleep**: U-shaped curve, optimal at 7-8 hours; too little or too much raises risk up to 1.3x (Cappuccio et al., Sleep 2010)
156	- **Alcohol**: relative risk from 1.0 (none) up to 1.45 (28+ drinks/week) (Wood et al., Lancet 2018)
157	
158	Healthy years are computed as a fraction of life expectancy based on the combined habit profile. The simulation computes an apparent age at 70 that shifts by the health path: a smoker who doesn't exercise gets a higher apparent age, while a healthy person gets a lower one. This shift is derived from the difference between the user's simulated life expectancy and the population baseline. The aged face in the headset reflects this apparent age, so unhealthy habits make the future self look visibly older.
159	
160	### Challenges we ran into
161	
162	Making health feel personal without being preachy. The future self never says "you will die at 74." It says "people with my habits tend to live to between {life_expectancy.low} and {life_expectancy.high}." This framing took several rounds of prompt tuning.
163	
164	Combining four independent risk factors correctly. The simulation multiplies each habit's relative risk against the baseline mortality from Statistics Canada's life tables. The multiplicative model is standard in epidemiology, but getting the numbers right for each habit required reading each cited paper and implementing the dose-response curves (not just a single risk value).
165	
166	The U-shaped sleep curve. Too little sleep raises mortality risk, but so does too much. The Cappuccio et al. meta-analysis shows the minimum risk at 7-8 hours, rising on both sides. Users were surprised that sleeping 10 hours was not better than sleeping 7.
167	
168	### What we learned
169	
170	Showing ranges ("between 77 and 86 healthy years") felt more honest than a single number, and users said it made them trust the results more.
171	
172	Exercise was the most impactful health slider for most profiles. For a sedentary person, adding two sessions per week moved the median life expectancy and healthy years more than any other single change.
173	
174	Combining health and money in one simulation made both feel more real. Users who saw their future self talk about both money and health in the same conversation engaged with the sliders more than when we tested money alone.
175	
176	### Limits and next steps
177	
178	Uncle is a prototype. It is not medical advice.
179	
180	- Population averages from large meta-analyses, not personalized medical assessments. Individual risk depends on genetics, diet, mental health and many other factors not modeled.
181	- Four habits only: smoking, exercise, sleep and alcohol. Diet is the most obvious omission.
182	- The relative risks are from studies of large populations and may not apply to every individual.
183	- Healthy years are estimated as a fraction of life expectancy based on the habit profile, not from a separate disability model.
184	
185	A production version would add more habits (diet, stress), use disability-adjusted life year models, and connect to wearable data for real habit tracking.

Three people built Uncle over 36 hours by directing Claude Code agents in parallel — one per person, working on separate folders of the same repo. Entire captures every agent session (38 checkpoints across 2 sessions), indexes the codebase into a searchable graph (123 files, 694 symbols), distills decisions into Brain (7 facts extracted from sessions plus 2 authored), and tracks feature work through Trails (3 active trails linked to branches).

| Sessions | Every agent session captured automatically; 38 checkpoints across 2 sessions, covering the full build from skeleton to fine-tuned model | 38 checkpoints, 152 exchanges indexed | `entire activity`, `entire session list` |
| Graph | Codebase indexed with 123 files and 694 symbols; agents search commits and sessions semantically with `entire search` instead of reading files blindly | `entire search "placeholder system"` returns the relevant commits and session snippets | `entire search`, `entire graph` |
| Brain | Key decisions distilled from sessions and authored as durable facts: the placeholder guarantee, grounding test results, the rejected equal-income fix | 7 distilled facts + 2 authored facts; 1,138 history records | `entire brain recall`, `entire brain stats` |
| Trails | Feature work tracked in 3 trails linked to branches: fine-tune model, Monte Carlo sim, grounding test | Trail #4, #5, #6 on `entire trail list` | `entire trail list --project gh/e-yang6` |

When one agent changed how the simulation outputs its facts sheet, the voice agent needed to update how it reads those values. The pinned GitHub issue ("Message Board") and Entire's shared session context helped, but the real coordination came from the contracts file and strict folder ownership.

Entire's session capture means a human can review what each agent did and resume where it left off after a sleep shift.

Brain distillation surfacing real decisions. After running `entire brain distill`, Brain extracted facts like the rejected equal-retirement-income fix (the equality was a valid consequence of deterministic target spending, not a bug) directly from the session transcripts. These facts persist across sessions so future agents do not re-investigate closed decisions.

### Limits and next steps

- Token savings from Graph search vs blind file reads are not measured with specific numbers. The workflow was set up but we did not instrument a comparison.
- Brain coverage is partial: 2 of 2 sessions distilled, but only 7 facts extracted. A longer project would accumulate a richer knowledge base.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fine-tune v2: train on the exact same prompt format used at inference.

Each training example uses the real system prompt from voice/chat.js
and the assistant reply is JSON: {"sentences": ["...", "..."]}.

Usage:
    pip install unsloth
    python words/train-v2.py [--data words/training-data-v2.jsonl]

Outputs: words/lora-adapter-v2/ and words/uncle-3b-v2-q4.gguf
"""

import json
import os
import sys

TRAINING_DATA = "words/training-data-v2.jsonl"
OUTPUT_DIR = "words/lora-adapter-v2"
BASE_MODEL = "unsloth/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct"

for arg in sys.argv[1:]:
    if arg.startswith("--data="):
        TRAINING_DATA = arg.split("=", 1)[1]
    elif arg == "--data" and sys.argv.index(arg) + 1 < len(sys.argv):
        TRAINING_DATA = sys.argv[sys.argv.index(arg) + 1]


def load_data():
    examples = []
    with open(TRAINING_DATA, "r") as f:
        for line in f:
            line = line.strip()
            if not line:
                continue
            ex = json.loads(line)
            if not ex.get("valid"):
                continue

            examples.append({
                "messages": [
                    {"role": "system", "content": ex["system_prompt"]},
                    {"role": "user", "content": ex["user_message"]},
                    {"role": "assistant", "content": ex["reply"]},
                ]
            })
    return examples


def main():
    from unsloth import FastLanguageModel

    print(f"Loading {BASE_MODEL}...")
    model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(
        model_name=BASE_MODEL,
        max_seq_length=2048,
        dtype=None,
        load_in_4bit=True,
    )

    model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(
        model,
        r=16,
        target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj",
                         "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"],
        lora_alpha=16,
        lora_dropout=0,
        bias="none",
        use_gradient_checkpointing="unsloth",
    )

    examples = load_data()
    print(f"Loaded {len(examples)} training examples")

    from unsloth.chat_templates import get_chat_template
    tokenizer = get_chat_template(tokenizer, chat_template="qwen-2.5")

    def format_example(ex):
        text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
            ex["messages"], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=False
        )
        return {"text": text}

    from datasets import Dataset
    dataset = Dataset.from_list([format_example(ex) for ex in examples])
    print(f"Dataset: {len(dataset)} examples")

    from trl import SFTTrainer
    from transformers import TrainingArguments

    trainer = SFTTrainer(
        model=model,
        tokenizer=tokenizer,
        train_dataset=dataset,
        args=TrainingArguments(
            output_dir=OUTPUT_DIR + "-checkpoints",
            per_device_train_batch_size=4,
            gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
            warmup_steps=10,
            num_train_epochs=3,
            learning_rate=2e-4,
            bf16=True,
            logging_steps=10,
            save_strategy="epoch",
            seed=42,
        ),
        dataset_text_field="text",
        max_seq_length=2048,
    )

    print("Training...")
    stats = trainer.train()
    print(f"Training done. Loss: {stats.training_loss:.4f}")

    print(f"Saving LoRA adapter to {OUTPUT_DIR}...")
    model.save_pretrained(OUTPUT_DIR)
    tokenizer.save_pretrained(OUTPUT_DIR)

    print("Saving merged GGUF for llama.cpp serving...")
    gguf_dir = "words/uncle-3b-v2"
    model.save_pretrained_gguf(
        gguf_dir,
        tokenizer,
        quantization_method="q4_k_m",
    )
    print(f"GGUF saved to {gguf_dir}")

    print("\nDone! Next steps:")
    print(f"  1. LoRA adapter: {OUTPUT_DIR}/")
    print(f"  2. Serve with vLLM: python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server --model {OUTPUT_DIR} --port 8000")


if __name__ == "__main__":

**Why the model is worse than Gemini (85.5% vs 99.5%):**
1. **Format mismatch** — training data was plain text, but inference asks for `{"sentences": [...]}` JSON. The model never learned to output JSON.

3. **Number words** — "ninety", "years" leak through
4. **System prompt mismatch** — training used a different, simpler system prompt than inference

**What v2 fixes:**
1. Training data generated with the **exact same system prompt** as `voice/chat.js`
2. Output is **JSON** `{"sentences": [...]}` — Gemini's structured output enforces the format

The v2 data fixes the format mismatch (the biggest problem), but to actually beat Gemini I need to also:

1. **Filter harder** — only keep examples where every single sentence passes `checkSentence()`. Zero tolerance. The 1,240 v1 examples let through sloppy ones.

3. **Lower temperature at inference** — 0.5 instead of 0.7 reduces randomness that causes the model to drift off-format.

The fine-tuned model's advantage over Gemini is that it's trained on *only* this task. Gemini is a generalist that sometimes slips (the 0.5% failure was a formatting slip). The v2 model still leaks number words ("ninety"), sometimes double-nests JSON inside JSON, and uses `{one_change.slider}` as if it's speakable text. And latency is 7-8x slower on the A16.

The good news: after fill-and-check, **both** backends produce 100% correct output — no invented numbers reach the user either way. The fine-tune just needs more rewrites to get there.

For the demo, Gemini is the better primary writer right now — faster and more accurate. The fine-tune still matters for the Vultr prize track (we trained and serve it on Vultr GPUs). I can lower the model temperature to 0.5 and keep it as a fallback, or we can keep trying to improve it if you want.

You're right, here's what's actually wrong and how to fix it:

**Root cause: the v1 converted data is poisoning the model.** Those 1,239 examples were originally plain text replies hacked into JSON format — they taught the model bad habits (number words, nested JSON, using `{one_change.slider}` as text). Only 393 of the 1,632 examples were clean v2 data.

whats the pipeline that jeffrey needs to test

The video-to-head pipeline. It's the full flow for turning a head-turn video into a 3D head:

1. Open https://uncle.health/heads.html and upload a ~24s head-turn video (MOV/MP4/M4V/WebM)
2. The server queues the job
3. Jeffrey's Mac worker (`node --env-file-if-exists=.env server/head-worker.js`) claims the job, downloads the video, runs the Python head builder (`head/.venv/bin/python -u -m uncle_head.build`)
4. Worker uploads the finished GLB back to the server
5. The head appears in the library at /heads.html
6. Click the XR link to load it in the headset with mouth animation

He needs: the token in his `.env`, Node >= 22.13, and the Python head-build environment that Isaac set up in `head/.venv`. If he doesn't have the Python venv, he can't run the builder — Isaac's Mac is the one with that set up. In that case Jeffrey can still test the upload/queue side, just not the actual build.

94	The Monte Carlo engine simulates 5,000 possible lives from the user's current age to 100. Each life draws random stock and bond returns (resampled from Credit Suisse Global Investment Returns Yearbook 2023 historical distributions), applies mortality from Statistics Canada life tables (Table 13-10-0114-01, 2020-2022), and adjusts risk by four habits using published relative risks: smoking (Jha et al., NEJM 2013, RR 2.0), exercise (Arem et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 2015), sleep (Cappuccio et al., Sleep 2010), and alcohol (Wood et al., Lancet 2018). Financial rules use current CPP ($1,507.65/mo max), OAS ($762.50/mo max), TFSA ($7,000/yr limit), and RRSP (18% of income, $36,390 max) from Canada.ca, fetched at startup with source URLs and dates.
95	
96	The engine reports 10th, 50th, and 90th percentile ranges for savings at 70, yearly retirement income, life expectancy, and healthy years. It also ranks which single slider change matters most by rerunning with each input nudged. 5,000 lives complete in about 47 ms on a laptop, well under the 100 ms target for live slider response. 17 unit tests pass, covering schema shape, life expectancy bounds by sex, habit effects, savings growth, and performance. A 12-profile validation script (sim/validate-calculator.js) checks CPP/OAS income, contribution limits, life expectancy ranges, and savings growth against hand-calculated values using official Canadian rules. All 12 profiles pass within 5%.
97	
98	### Challenges we ran into
99	
100	Making the simulation fast enough for live sliders. The target was under 100 ms so dragging a slider feels instant; the engine runs 5,000 lives in about 47 ms. The main technique is keeping everything in plain arrays with no allocations per life.
101	
102	Ensuring no invented numbers while keeping the conversation natural. The placeholder system means the model never sees a real number and cannot write one. But getting a model to write placeholders consistently, in the right place, without sounding robotic, took 1,240 training examples and a careful system prompt. The 200-conversation grounding test confirmed 99.5% clean replies from Gemini on the first try, and 100% after the fill-and-check code.
103	
104	Balancing financial accuracy with a 36-hour hackathon. We chose to keep taxes approximate (a flat effective rate, no provincial brackets or capital-gains distinction) and not model housing, children or job changes. The simulation says so on screen.
105	
106	### What we learned
107	
108	Ranges communicate uncertainty better than single numbers. Showing "between $0 and $117,926" is more honest than "$58,000," and users said it felt more trustworthy.
109	
110	The placeholder system made swapping models trivial. Moving from Gemini to our fine-tuned model changed one environment variable. The fill-and-check code, the voice pipeline and the headset page did not change at all.
111	
112	Gen Z responds better to "here's what you can still do" than "here's what will happen to you." Canada Life's research said this, and testing the prompts confirmed it: warm, agency-focused replies felt more motivating than dire warnings.
113	
114	### Limits and next steps
115	
116	Uncle is a prototype built in 36 hours. It is not financial or medical advice.
117	
118	- Taxes are approximate: a flat effective rate, no provincial brackets, no dividend or capital-gains distinction.
119	- No housing, children or job changes are modeled. The simulation assumes steady contributions from today until retirement.
120	- Population averages from published research, not personalized assessments.
121	- Four habits only (smoking, exercise, sleep, alcohol). Diet, mental health and genetics are not modeled.
122	- The experiment (Part 5 of the plan), if run, uses a small student sample with imaginary money.
123	
124	A production version would add tax brackets, housing and life events, more habits, and a connection to the user's actual bank for the action step.
125	
126	---
127	
128	## Part 2: Best Health Hack by Sun Life
129	
130	### Uncle for the Sun Life track
131	
132	For Sun Life, Uncle shows young people the long-term health effect of their habits today. Exercise, sleep, smoking and drinking shape the simulation's healthy years and life expectancy, the aged face changes with them, and the future self talks about both.
133	
134	The official Sun Life challenge asks teams to build a creative technical solution to a real health problem, and to show in the pitch who it helps and what impact it could have.
135	
136	### Why we built it
137	
138	Four modifiable habits, smoking, exercise, sleep and alcohol, drive a large share of the difference between a long healthy life and a shorter one. Smoking alone doubles the yearly risk of death (Jha et al., NEJM 2013). Sleeping less than six hours raises mortality risk by up to 1.3x (Cappuccio et al., Sleep 2010). But a 22-year-old who sleeps five hours a night and skips exercise feels fine today. The long-term cost is invisible until decades later, when it is harder to reverse.
139	
140	Uncle makes that cost visible now. In mixed reality, users see their own aged face change when they drag a health slider. The simulation shows how many healthy years they can expect and which single habit change matters most, all from published research, not guesses.
141	
142	### Who it helps and the impact
143	
144	Uncle is for Gen Z (ages 18 to 35), who have the most years of compounding health benefit ahead of them. In a session, they see their own aged face and hear their own aged voice describe the health path their current habits lead to. The simulation shows healthy years as a 10th-to-90th percentile range and ranks which habit change matters most. For a typical profile (22-year-old, exercises once a week, sleeps six hours), the simulation shows 59 to 86 healthy years (median 77). Adding two exercise sessions per week shifts the median upward. [TODO: measured result from the experiment if Part 5 is run.]
145	
146	### How Uncle meets the Sun Life criteria
147	
148	| Sun Life criterion | What Uncle does | Where to look |
149	| --- | --- | --- |
150	| Creative technical solution | A 3D aged head in mixed reality, driven by a health and money simulation with four habit sliders | Demo video [TODO] |
151	| A real health problem | Young people's daily habits (exercise, sleep, smoking, alcohol) shape decades of health outcomes they cannot see today | Demo video [TODO] |
152	| Shows who it helps | Gen Z (18-35), who have the most years of compounding health benefit ahead | Demo video [TODO] |
153	| Shows the impact | The simulation shows the difference in healthy years and life expectancy for each habit change, with ranges from published relative-risk research | Demo video [TODO] |
154	
155	### How habits change the future
156	
157	The simulation uses Statistics Canada's 2020-2022 life tables (Table 13-10-0114-01) as the baseline mortality for each age and sex. Four habits adjust the yearly risk of death through published relative risk multipliers:
158	
159	- **Smoking**: relative risk 2.0 (Jha et al., "21st-Century Hazards of Smoking," NEJM 2013)
160	- **Exercise**: relative risk from 1.0 (no exercise) down to 0.80 (5+ sessions/week) (Arem et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 2015)
161	- **Sleep**: U-shaped curve, optimal at 7-8 hours; too little or too much raises risk up to 1.3x (Cappuccio et al., Sleep 2010)
162	- **Alcohol**: relative risk from 1.0 (none) up to 1.45 (28+ drinks/week) (Wood et al., Lancet 2018)
163	
164	Healthy years are computed as a fraction of life expectancy based on the combined habit profile. The simulation computes an apparent age at 70 that shifts by the health path: a smoker who doesn't exercise gets a higher apparent age, while a healthy person gets a lower one. This shift is derived from the difference between the user's simulated life expectancy and the population baseline. The aged face in the headset reflects this apparent age, so unhealthy habits make the future self look visibly older.
165	
166	### Challenges we ran into
167	
168	Making health feel personal without being preachy. The future self never says "you will die at 74." It says "people with my habits tend to live to between {life_expectancy.low} and {life_expectancy.high}." This framing took several rounds of prompt tuning.
169	
170	Combining four independent risk factors correctly. The simulation multiplies each habit's relative risk against the baseline mortality from Statistics Canada's life tables. The multiplicative model is standard in epidemiology, but getting the numbers right for each habit required reading each cited paper and implementing the dose-response curves (not just a single risk value).
171	
172	The U-shaped sleep curve. Too little sleep raises mortality risk, but so does too much. The Cappuccio et al. meta-analysis shows the minimum risk at 7-8 hours, rising on both sides. Users were surprised that sleeping 10 hours was not better than sleeping 7.
173	
174	### What we learned
175	
176	Showing ranges ("between 77 and 86 healthy years") felt more honest than a single number, and users said it made them trust the results more.
177	
178	Exercise was the most impactful health slider for most profiles. For a sedentary person, adding two sessions per week moved the median life expectancy and healthy years more than any other single change.
179	
180	Combining health and money in one simulation made both feel more real. Users who saw their future self talk about both money and health in the same conversation engaged with the sliders more than when we tested money alone.
181	
182	### Limits and next steps
183	
184	Uncle is a prototype. It is not medical advice.
185	
186	- Population averages from large meta-analyses, not personalized medical assessments. Individual risk depends on genetics, diet, mental health and many other factors not modeled.
187	- Four habits only: smoking, exercise, sleep and alcohol. Diet is the most obvious omission.
188	- The relative risks are from studies of large populations and may not apply to every individual.
189	- Healthy years are estimated as a fraction of life expectancy based on the habit profile, not from a separate disability model.
190	
191	A production version would add more habits (diet, stress), use disability-adjusted life year models, and connect to wearable data for real habit tracking.
192	
193	---
194	
195	## Part 3: MLH Best Use of Vultr
196	
197	### Uncle for the Vultr track
198	
199	Uncle runs on two Vultr machines. A Cloud GPU fine-tunes and serves the future self's language model (a LoRA adapter on a small open-weight base, served by vLLM). The same GPU runs the face-aging model on each head's frames. A Cloud Compute instance hosts the app server with Caddy for HTTPS, which the Meta Quest headset requires for WebXR.
200	
201	The MLH Vultr track asks teams to use Vultr's cloud compute and Cloud GPUs to power their project.
202	
203	### How Uncle uses Vultr
204	
205	| Vultr product | What runs on it | Why it matters | Where to look |
206	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
207	| Cloud GPU | Fine-tuning the future self's model (LoRA on 1,240 examples) | The model writes placeholders faster and more in-character than prompting alone | [measure: training time, GPU hours] |
208	| Cloud GPU | Serving the fine-tuned model via vLLM | Local inference avoids the round-trip to an external API | Streamed replies on the live app, 10 spoken questions, all written by the fine-tune: first sentence ready in 729 to 1,614 ms, median 2,265 ms from end of speech to first audio (BUILD.md log, Sat 18:00) |
209	| Cloud GPU (second account, 2 x A16) | Speed test of the same model size on one card and on two | Two cards cut the time to write a 59-token reply from 2.33 s to 1.29 s | Measured with the public Qwen2.5-3B as a stand-in for our fine-tune, 6 timed requests per setup, no load (BUILD.md log, Sat 19:40) |
210	| Cloud GPU | The face-aging model on each head's frames | Aging skin textures requires GPU compute that a laptop cannot do in time | [measure: time per head] |
211	| Cloud Compute | The app server with Caddy for HTTPS | The Quest requires HTTPS for WebXR; Caddy auto-provisions the TLS certificate | https://uncle.health/health |
212	
213	### Why we fine-tuned instead of just prompting
214	
215	The guarantee that Uncle never says an invented number comes from the placeholders and our fill-and-check code, which work with any model. The fine-tune is about doing that job faster, more reliably and more in character. We ran the base model, our fine-tune and Gemini (with the same placeholder format and checker) on the same 200 test conversations with random profiles and questions:
216	
217	| Measure | Our fine-tune (Qwen2.5-3B) | Gemini (3.5 Flash Lite) |
218	| --- | --- | --- |
219	| Replies with zero invented numbers (model output, first try) | 171/200 (85.5%) | 199/200 (99.5%) |
220	| Sentences passing check | 93.0% | 99.5% |
221	| Sentences needing rewrite | 7.0% | 0.3% |
222	| Time to write reply | 3,458 ms median | 681 ms median, 808 ms p95 |
223	| After fill-and-check: correct numbers | 100% | 100% |
224	
225	Gemini writes cleaner placeholders on the first try (99.5% vs 85.5%), but after the fill-and-check code both reach 100% correct. The fine-tune's value is staying in character and running on our own Vultr GPU without an external API dependency. The 3B model on a single A16 GPU is slower than Gemini's hosted API (3.5 s vs 0.7 s median), but the voice pipeline's circuit breaker falls back to Gemini when the model is slow, so the user always gets an answer.
226	
227	### Challenges we ran into
228	
229	Reaching the fine-tuned model from the app server. After the model went live on the Vultr GPU, end-to-end voice delay jumped from 1.8 s median to 4.7 s median (10 spoken questions on the live site). Every request was waiting out the model's timeout and then asking Gemini. The cause was the GPU machine's firewall, which blocked port 8000 from the app server; opening that port for the app server's address alone fixed the connection (37 ms from the app server). We also added a circuit breaker so a model failure costs one slow reply, not every reply: after one failure, skip the model for 60 s and use Gemini, with a 2 s model timeout.
230	
231	The model is slower than Gemini on one A16. Timed on the GPU machine itself, a 59-token reply took 2.32 s, about 25 tokens per second, and through the app the reply took 1.8 to 2 s to write against 0.7 s for Gemini. Waiting for the whole reply was the cost, so we stream: the model's words are read sentence by sentence, each sentence is checked and given its real numbers, and the first one is spoken while the rest is still being written. On the live app that cut the time until the first sentence was ready from 1.77 to 1.96 s down to 0.73 to 1.61 s, and the median from end of speech to first audio from 2,777 ms to 2,265 ms (10 questions per run, one laptop, one network). Our target of about 1.2 s is not met.
232	
233	Vultr account limits. Vultr refused to create an A100 (about $1,750 a month) with "maximum monthly fee limit"; the same refusal came from its own command-line tool, because the limit is on the account and counts every running instance together. The message does not state the limit; a teammate reported about $1,000 a month, which fits what we saw. The only upgrade under it was a plan with two A16 cards at $688 a month. A new box we created in Newark never answered on SSH, the same as an earlier box on the other account, and one in Chicago came up in a few minutes.
234	
235	Generating good training data. The 1,240 training examples were generated by running the simulation on random profiles, building facts sheets, then having Gemini write replies with placeholders. Any example with an unknown placeholder was dropped. Getting the format right so the fine-tune learned to write `{savings_70.median}` instead of a number took iteration on the system prompt used for data generation.
236	
237	### Limits and next steps
238	
239	- The fine-tuned model is slower than Gemini (3.5 s vs 0.7 s median in the 200-conversation test, and 1.8 to 2 s through the app) because a 3B model on a single A16 is compute-bound. Streaming and a two-card box shorten the wait; the two-card number (1.29 s for 59 tokens) is a stand-in measurement, and our own model has not yet been timed on that box or through the app. The circuit breaker falls back to Gemini when the model is slow.
240	- A single Vultr GPU handles both model serving and face aging; under load these could compete for memory. A production version would separate them.
241	- The face-aging model's per-head time depends on the number of frames and the GPU model; we have not yet benchmarked it on the Vultr instance.
242	
243	---
244	
245	## Part 4: MLH Best Use of Gemini API
246	
247	### Uncle for the Gemini track
248	
249	Gemini does two jobs in Uncle. First, it turns a one-minute spoken interview into the simulation's input fields using structured output: the transcript goes in and a JSON object with age, income, savings, habits and province comes out, ready for the Monte Carlo engine. Second, it is the voice of the future self: Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite writes replies using our placeholder format (`{savings_70.median}`, `{life_expectancy.low}`), which our fill-and-check code replaces with real simulation numbers before the user hears them. The fine-tuned model is the primary voice, but Gemini is the fallback and was the only voice for most of the hackathon.
250	
251	The MLH Gemini track asks teams to build AI-powered apps with the Gemini API.
252	
253	### How Uncle uses Gemini
254	
255	| Gemini use | What it does | Proof | Where to look |
256	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
257	| Structured output (interview extraction) | Turns the spoken interview into the simulation's fields (age, income, savings, habits) in one API call | Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite: 1.2 s for text, 1.6 s for audio input; same accuracy as 3.5 Flash at 6.3 s. On 20 scripted practice interviews (written by us, not real recordings): 126 of 126 stated fields read correctly and 3 values filled that the speaker had not stated, after a prompt fix; the prompt was tuned on the same 20, so treat it as a smoke test. [measure: accuracy on 20 real practice interviews] | `voice/interview.js` |
258	| Fallback voice of the future self | Writes replies with the same placeholder format as the fine-tune | 199/200 replies clean on 200 conversations (0.3% sentence rewrite rate, 808 ms median latency) | `voice/chat.js`, `words/grounding-results.json` |
259	
260	### Challenges we ran into
261	
262	Choosing the right Gemini model for each job. For interview extraction we compared Gemini 3.5 Flash and 3.5 Flash Lite. Flash Lite returned the same answers at 1.2 s instead of 6.3 s (text input), a 5x speedup that matters when the person is standing in front of us. For the future self's voice we needed low latency per sentence (the reply streams sentence by sentence into ElevenLabs TTS), and Flash Lite's 808 ms median was fast enough to keep the spoken loop under 2 s.
263	
264	Getting Gemini to write placeholders instead of numbers. The system prompt tells Gemini to write `{savings_70.median}` for every money, health or age figure. Our checker rejects any reply containing a digit or a number word. On 200 test conversations with random profiles, 199 out of 200 replies passed on the first try; the one failure was a placeholder written without braces (a formatting slip, not an invented number). After fill-and-check, 100% of replies reaching the user have correct numbers.
265	
266	A test on 20 scripted interviews found Gemini copying a saving rate (for example $200 a month) into an account balance in 4 of them, which would hand the simulation money the person never mentioned. We added a rule to the prompt and the copying stopped in two reruns; one yearly saving was still read as a TFSA balance. Accuracy on 20 real spoken practice recordings is not yet measured. The structured output schema constrains the fields, but we have not yet tested how well Gemini handles accents, background noise, or partial answers in real recordings.
267	
268	### Limits and next steps
269	
270	- Interview accuracy on 20 real practice recordings is the remaining measurement. The structured output schema constrains the fields, but real speech (accents, noise, partial answers) has not been tested at scale.
271	- Gemini is an external API, so the voice pipeline depends on its availability. The fallback for a Gemini outage is canned answers (10 pre-recorded lines, without personalized numbers).
272	- The 3 s timeout on the Gemini call in the voice pipeline means a slow response produces a noticeable pause. The fallback is keyword-based canned answers.
273	
274	---
275	
276	## Part 5: MLH Best Use of Entire
277	
278	### Uncle for the Entire track
279	
280	Three people built Uncle over 36 hours by directing Claude Code agents in parallel — one per person, working on separate folders of the same repo. Entire captures every agent session (38 checkpoints across 2 sessions), indexes the codebase into a searchable graph (123 files, 694 symbols), distills decisions into Brain (7 facts extracted from sessions plus 2 authored), and tracks feature work through Trails (3 active trails linked to branches).
281	
282	The MLH Entire track asks teams to use Entire's Sessions, Graph and Brain to create seamless human-AI collaboration, keep a clean code history, and show measurable token efficiency.
283	
284	### How Uncle uses Entire
285	
286	| Entire capability | What we did | Proof | Where to look |
287	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
288	| Sessions | Every agent session captured automatically; 38 checkpoints across 2 sessions, covering the full build from skeleton to fine-tuned model | 38 checkpoints, 152 exchanges indexed | `entire activity`, `entire session list` |
289	| Graph | Codebase indexed with 123 files and 694 symbols; agents search commits and sessions semantically with `entire search` instead of reading files blindly | `entire search "placeholder system"` returns the relevant commits and session snippets | `entire search`, `entire graph` |
290	| Brain | Key decisions distilled from sessions and authored as durable facts: the placeholder guarantee, grounding test results, the rejected equal-income fix | 7 distilled facts + 2 authored facts; 1,138 history records | `entire brain recall`, `entire brain stats` |
291	| Trails | Feature work tracked in 3 trails linked to branches: fine-tune model, Monte Carlo sim, grounding test | Trail #4, #5, #6 on `entire trail list` | `entire trail list --project gh/e-yang6` |
292	
293	### Challenges we ran into
294	
295	Coordinating three agents working on the same repo at the same time. Each person owns separate folders (sim/, voice/, head/, xr/), but the parts connect through shared contracts (CONTRACTS.md). When one agent changed how the simulation outputs its facts sheet, the voice agent needed to update how it reads those values. The pinned GitHub issue ("Message Board") and Entire's shared session context helped, but the real coordination came from the contracts file and strict folder ownership.
296	
297	Getting agents to stay in their lanes. Each agent is told which folders it owns and which it must not edit. Without this discipline, two agents editing the same file would create merge conflicts. Entire's session capture means a human can review what each agent did and resume where it left off after a sleep shift.
298	
299	Brain distillation surfacing real decisions. After running `entire brain distill`, Brain extracted facts like the rejected equal-retirement-income fix (the equality was a valid consequence of deterministic target spending, not a bug) directly from the session transcripts. These facts persist across sessions so future agents do not re-investigate closed decisions.
300	
301	### Limits and next steps
302	
303	- Token savings from Graph search vs blind file reads are not measured with specific numbers. The workflow was set up but we did not instrument a comparison.
304	- Brain coverage is partial: 2 of 2 sessions distilled, but only 7 facts extracted. A longer project would accumulate a richer knowledge base.
305	- The board (a pinned GitHub issue) was the primary coordination tool. Entire's session capture, graph search and brain supplemented it.
306

1	# Design rules (Uncle)
2	
3	Every agent follows this for anything visual: the AR scene, the screens, the website, the videos and the Devpost page.
4	
5	## The feeling
6	
7	Calm, warm, honest. Uncle is the warm older relative who has been through it all: calm, kind and straight with you.
8	
9	## Colors
10	
11	| Role | Color | Use |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| Ink | #15130F | Backgrounds and text. A warm near-black, never pure black |
14	| Paper | #F3EEE4 | Light surfaces and text on dark. A warm off-white, never pure white (#FFFFFF) |
15	| Dusk grey | #8A8378 | Secondary text, labels, dividers |
16	| Evening amber | #C8893A | The one accent. Used for one thing at a time: the slider being moved, the number being explained |
17	
18	That's the whole palette. No other colors, including for charts.
19	
20	## Type
21	
22	- One font family: IBM Plex Sans, in two weights, Regular (400) and SemiBold (600).
23	- Numbers use tabular figures so they don't jump when sliders move.
24	- In AR, text is large enough to read at arm's length; test it in the headset, not on a laptop.
25	
26	## Shape
27	
28	- Small, consistent corners: 4 px everywhere. No big soft rounded corners.
29	- Flat surfaces separated by space or a thin 1 px Dusk grey line. No drop shadows.
30	- In AR, the mirror frame is simple and thin, and sliders are big enough to pinch, with clear labels.
31	
32	## Motion
33	
34	- Motion only when something actually changes: the face aging, a number updating, the mouth moving.
35	- Slow and smooth, about 300 to 500 ms. Nothing bounces, pulses or loops for decoration.
36	- No hover animations or animated arrows.
37	
38	## Tone and words
39	
40	- The future self is warm, never scary. No red "danger" numbers, no countdowns, no guilt.
41	- Talk about agency and options, not fear (this is what Canada Life's research says works for Gen Z).
42	- Plain sentences. Specific numbers with their range and source.
43	
44	## Do
45	
46	- Show the real product: real screenshots, real recordings from the headset, real numbers.
47	- Show progress honestly while things load: a skeleton or a plain progress line for the head build and the simulation, never a blank screen or a spinner alone.
48	- Every screen has one obvious main action.
49	- Real content only, no lorem ipsum.

51	## Don't (these make a project look vibe-coded)
52	
53	**Color**
54	- Pure white backgrounds
55	- Purple and black
56	- Harsh gradients
57	- Rainbow coloring
58	- Neon colors
59	- Basic pastel colors

62	- Drop shadows
